physics.title: How radar finds water under trees
physics.lede: NISAR sends microwaves 24 cm long (L-band) and listens for the echo in two polarisations: HH, sent and received horizontally, and HV, sent horizontally and received vertically. The echo changes with what lies under the leaves.
physics.diagram_aria: Three scenes. Dry forest: the radar scatters in the leaves and a modest echo returns. Flooded forest: L-band passes the leaves, bounces off the water onto the trunks and returns strongly, while C-band stops in the leaves. Open water: the radar reflects away and almost nothing returns.
physics.sig_dry_title: Dry forest: scattering in the leaves
physics.sig_dry: HH is moderate, around −8 dB, and HV fairly strong. The gap between them stays small.
physics.sig_flooded: HH turns very bright, around −2 dB, while HV barely changes, so the gap grows past 7 dB.
physics.sig_water: Both HH and HV are very dark, below about −16 and −22 dB.
physics.cband: Sentinel-1 uses C-band waves about 5.6 cm long. The leaves at the top of the canopy scatter most of them, so under closed forest C-band rarely reaches the water. We compare against OPERA's C-band water map including its own flooded-vegetation class, so the gap we report is what C-band misses at its best.
physics.confidence: A spot is hatched as low confidence when its numbers sit within a margin of a threshold, or when its neighbours disagree. Days flooded counts low-confidence passes at half weight.
physics.rule_water: Open water: HH below {hh} dB and HV below {hv} dB.
physics.rule_flooded: Water under vegetation: on trees, shrubs or wetland, HH above {hh} dB and more than {ratio} dB above HV.
physics.rule_built: Built-up areas are left out, because buildings produce the same double bounce.
physics.rule_low: Low confidence: within {margin} dB of a threshold, or neighbours spread by more than {spread} dB.
physics.limit_1: Thresholds start from published L-band studies and are tuned per site against a few labelled points. They are not trained on ground truth.
physics.limit_2: Flooding under very dense, tall canopy can still be missed, and flooding under sparse shrubs can look like dry grass. Both show as low confidence.
physics.limit_3: Built-up areas are excluded, because buildings mimic the double-bounce signal.
physics.limit_4: NISAR revisits every 12 days, or 6 with both orbit directions, so short flash floods between passes can be missed.
physics.limit_5: Agreement with river gauges shows the timing is right, not that every pixel is right.
physics.limit_6: Population figures are WorldPop model estimates, not a census.

motion.layer_los: Track {track} {dir}: motion toward or away from the satellite
motion.layer_rate_los: Track {track} {dir}: speed toward or away from the satellite
motion.layer_total: Track {track} {dir}: total motion since the first date
motion.key_rate: A speed fitted through every date of the season, given per year as in the literature. Bars: how many cells have each speed; the band is 2σ of the speed on the stable reference.
motion.fringe_key: Each full colour cycle is {cm} cm of motion: count the cycles from a still area to read the total.
motion.lead_quake: M{mag}, {date}: from {n} radar geometries, NISAR measured the ground moving as much as about {west} cm west and {east} cm east on either side of the fault (1st and 99th percentiles of the cells).
motion.lead_quake_los: M{mag} earthquake, {n} radar geometries: pick one to see its line-of-sight motion.
motion.lead_sinking: Between {start} and {end}, parts of the city sank at up to {rate} cm a year (1st percentile of the cells): {km2} km² faster than 10 cm a year and {km2_2} km² faster than 20 cm. Typical uncertainty of the vertical speed: ±{sigma} cm a year (1σ).
motion.lead_sinking_los: Line-of-sight motion from one radar geometry; the vertical speed needs an ascending and a descending track.
motion.geom_quake: Track {track} {dir}, {start} to {end}: {angle}° from the vertical, coherence {coh}, {pct}% of the area measured; noise in the pair before the quake ±{noise} cm.
motion.geom_chain: Track {track} {dir}, {start} to {end}: {n} consecutive 12-day pairs, {angle}° from the vertical, coherence {coh}, {pct}% measured; speed on the stable reference ±{spread} cm a year (1σ).
motion.note_quake: Referenced to {ref}, which may itself have moved a few centimetres. The phase is corrected for the ionosphere with the product's own screen; the troposphere is not removed. Kept where coherence is at least {coh} and in the main unwrapped area of each frame. North–south motion is not resolved: these orbits barely see it.
motion.note_sinking: Referenced to {ref}. Each 12-day pair is corrected for the ionosphere and, on the hills, for water vapour that follows terrain height; each date still carries a few centimetres of weather, while the speed is fitted to all of them. Kept where coherence is at least {coh}; a cell lost in one pair stays out after it. The pairs form one chain with no closed loops, so unwrapping errors cannot be checked by loop closure.

legend.burn_caption: Burned forest (HH over HV up {rise} dB, lasting), by the pass that first saw it
legend.burn_note: Where a forest burns, the radar's HV echo from needles and branches falls while HH from the trunks and the ground holds or rises, so HH over HV goes up. Seen through smoke, cloud and night; dark red burned first.
burn.title: Burned forest, seen through the smoke
burn.lead: Between {first} and {last}, NISAR's HH over HV rose by {rise} dB or more and stayed up over {km2} km² of the {forest} km² of forest in this box ({name}).
burn.lead_none: No forest here saw its HH over HV rise {rise} dB and stay up this season.
burn.check_none: No independent burned-area map is available for this box yet.
burn.held_out: The {rise} dB threshold was chosen on the west half of this box; on the east half, which it never saw, F1 is {f1} (found {recall}%, right {precision}%).
burn.held_out_other: The {rise} dB threshold was chosen on {tuned} and not changed here, so every score on this card is from forest it never saw.
burn.sweep_caption: How the answer depends on the rise that counts as burned (the bold row is used):
burn.smoke: The camera on the same passes (share of the box its cloud mask kept; thin smoke is often not flagged): {list}. The radar needs no clear sky.
burn.note: A rising HH over HV means the canopy's volume echo was lost: fire, logging and windthrow look alike to the radar, and so does water rising under trees (see above). The map says which pass first saw it, not why. Rain moves HH and HV together, which the ratio cancels; one bright pass alone is not counted. Forest = vegetation in ESA WorldCover that GEDI does not measure below 5 m.
burn.ref_months_later: {short} months in the check: {list}. NISAR first saw {km2} km² after them; {short} has not mapped that time yet, so it is scored against the last month.
burn.other_check: Also against {ref} ({list}): it marks {ref_km2} km² burned; F1 {f1} (found {recall}%, right {precision}%).
burn.af_lead: NASA's VIIRS imagers ({sensors}) saw {n} fire pixels here from {first} to {last}, several times a day; the strongest gave off {frp} MW.
burn.af_show: Show where VIIRS saw fire since the last radar pass (yellow points)
burn.af_dates: Where both saw fire ({cells} cells of about 500 m), VIIRS's first sighting fell between NISAR's pass before and the pass that found the burn in {within}% of cells, and on or before that pass in {before}%; the radar saw it a median {lead} days after VIIRS.
burn.af_dates_none: No cell is called burned by both NISAR and VIIRS, so their dates cannot be compared here.
burn.af_note: VIIRS sees the heat of a burning fire, through smoke but not thick cloud, at 375 m; NISAR sees the forest that is left, every 12 days. A missing day can mean cloud, not a quiet fire. Fire pixels of low confidence are drawn but not used in the date check.

checks.title: How we know the ground moved
checks.jpl_lead: JPL's NISAR team processed {n} of the same pairs for the USGS fault model, and USGS published the points. Against them, ours correlate at r = {rmin}–{rmax} and differ by {dmin}–{dmax} cm (root mean square, after a constant: the two use different stable references). Our amplitudes are {smin}–{smax}% larger; the ionosphere correction is the likeliest difference.
checks.model_lead: {label}, Mw {mw}, built from {data}. We computed the surface motion of its slip with Okada's (1985) equations and projected it on each radar geometry.
checks.model_used: On the {n} tracks USGS used, the model matches our maps at r = {rmin}–{rmax}, residual {emin}–{emax} cm (root mean square).
checks.model_held: Track {track} was not used by USGS: a test the model never saw. There it matches at r = {r}, residual {e} cm against {obs} cm of signal.
checks.model_sides: Radar minus model on that track, median: {west} cm west of the M{mag} epicentre, {east} cm east of it.
checks.show_resid: Show radar minus model for track {track}
checks.model_limits: Limits: a uniform elastic half-space (Poisson's ratio {nu}) where USGS used a layered crust, so amplitudes differ by a few per cent; the model's patches are 10 km across, so it cannot follow motion that changes over a few kilometres.
checks.show_slip: Show the USGS slip on the map (darker = more slip)
checks.gnss_none: No GNSS station with data near these months.
checks.gnss_same: {id} measured its position every day over the same months ({start} to {end}): vertical speed {gnss} cm a year; NISAR {nisar} cm a year within 250 m. Along track {track}'s line of sight: GNSS {glos}, NISAR {nlos} cm a year.
checks.scatter_aria: GNSS vertical speed against NISAR vertical speed at each station
checks.key_earlier: an earlier year (the station stopped before NISAR's season)
checks.gnss_limits: GNSS daily positions from the Nevada Geodetic Laboratory (IGS20 frame). Their horizontal motion includes the plate's (under about 1.5 cm a year), which the radar, tied to nearby hills, does not: up to about 1 cm a year along the line of sight. An earlier year is context, not a test: the city's sinking changes slowly, but it does change.

landing.hero_title: The flood is under the trees. Only one kind of radar can see it.
landing.hero_lede: Cameras see clouds. Most radar sees leaves. NISAR's L-band radar, with a 24 cm wavelength, reaches the ground under forest, smoke and night. Under the Canopy maps what it finds: flood water hidden in forests, forest burned beneath the smoke, and ground that moved. Every number is checked against an independent measurement.

landing.challenge_quote: "Earth's surface is an endless dance of natural processes and human activities, but these changes are often difficult to visualize, understand, and communicate. From wetland loss to forest wildfires, earthquakes, farming activities, glacier movement, and more, Earth is in a constant waltz of surface changes. Your challenge is to build an interactive application that uses radar remote sensing data from the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission to track and visualize one or more types of surface change at locations around the world."

ice.speed_title: Can NISAR see the ice move?
ice.speed_test: NISAR's ice-offset product was tested on {pairs} pairs of passes: on bare rock, which does not move, it reads a median {noise} m a year; on the ice, its three measuring windows agree on only {agree}% of cells (at best {best}%).
ice.speed_compare: Where they agree, NISAR's best pair reads {nlo}–{nhi} m a year on the glaciers (its rock noise: {noise}), against {ilo}–{ihi} from ITS_LIVE.
ice.speed_why: That is a third to a half of the glaciers' speed, from the few cells that agree, where the ice moves least or the match locked onto rock and debris: NISAR's offsets do not follow these glaciers in summer. Small, slow glaciers whose surface melts and changes within 12 days lose the pattern the radar matches.
ice.speed_itslive_error: ITS_LIVE, from optical image pairs, has its own error of ±{lo}–{hi} m a year for one pair, so only the median of the summer's {n} pairs is steady.
ice.speed_caption: Speed in metres a year: ITS_LIVE median of the summer's pairs ± its own error for one pair, and NISAR's best pair ({track}, {start} to {end}) where its windows agree.
ice.show: Show the icefield on the map
ice.limits: What this does not say: that this fire's smoke caused a given amount of melt. A darker summer can also mean the snow melted off early, leaving bare ice, which is darker than snow; and thick smoke also blocks the sunlight that melts ice (Aubry-Wake et al. 2022). Smoke is the VIIRS Deep Blue aerosol depth of the 1° cell over the icefield (often missing over snow and cloud); brightness is VIIRS VNP43MA3 white-sky shortwave albedo, a daily value drawn from 16 days of views; glacier outlines are RGI 7.0 (mostly mapped in 2006).

guide.w_q: Is there water under these trees, and for how long?
guide.w_waves_aria: A 5.6 cm C-band wave meets leaves its own size and scatters; a 24 cm L-band wave passes them.
guide.w_c: C-band, 5.6 cm: scattered by the leaves
guide.w_chart_aria: HH across, HV up: the regions this site's thresholds call open water and water under trees, the low-confidence bands, and where the three typical echoes fall.
guide.w_pick_site: Pick a site to see its own thresholds drawn here.
guide.w_c_gauge_d: {name}: the mapped flood rises and falls with the river, r = {r} over {n} passes.
guide.w_c_swot_d: {n} SWOT overpasses of an independent satellite, compared with the mapped flood.
guide.w_c_cal_d: {pct} % balanced accuracy on labelled places the thresholds were not tuned on.
guide.w_c_cband_d: Compared with OPERA's C-band map including its own flooded-vegetation class, so the gap is what C-band misses at its best.
guide.f_q: Did the forest burn, even under smoke?
guide.f_aria: Before the fire, leaves scatter the radar and return a strong HV echo; after it, the trunks and ground answer in HH, so HH rises against HV.
guide.f_phys: Leaves and twigs scatter the radar every way and turn its polarisation, a strong HV echo. When fire takes the canopy, that echo goes, while the trunks and the ground still send HH back. Smoke is no obstacle: it is far smaller than a 24 cm wave.
guide.f_rule: Burned: HH − HV rises at least {db} dB above its level before the fire, on forest, in patches large enough to trust.
guide.f_rule2: The first pass that shows the rise dates the burn, so the map shows the fire's spread pass by pass.
guide.f_c_ref_d: Compared with MODIS and VIIRS burned area, maps the rule was not tuned on.
guide.f_c_dates_d: Where both call a cell burned, the burn day in NASA's map falls within one pass of when NISAR first saw it for {pct} % of cells; NISAR saw it a median {lag} days later.
guide.f_c_held_d: The rule was set on one half of the fire and checked on the other.
guide.f_lim3: Logging and windthrow also remove the canopy and look the same to the radar.
guide.g_q: How far did the ground move, and which way?
guide.g_aria: Two passes 12 days apart; the ground moved between them, so the path to the radar changed and the phase turned: a colour cycle for every 12 cm.
guide.g_phys: NISAR images the same place from the same orbit 12 days apart. If the ground moved towards or away from the radar, the echo's phase shifts: one full turn of colour, a fringe, for every 12 cm the round trip changes, half the 24 cm wavelength.
guide.g_rule1: Distance from phase: the change along the radar's line of sight is the phase × wavelength ÷ 4π, about 1.9 cm for each radian.
guide.g_rule2: Direction from geometry: tracks looking from different sides are combined by least squares into east–west and up–down motion, with its uncertainty.
guide.g_c_jpl_d: The same radar pairs, processed independently by NASA JPL, side by side on one colour scale.
guide.g_c_usgs_d: The earthquake's slip, modelled forward with Okada (1985), compared on a track the method never used.
guide.g_c_gnss_d: Stations that felt the motion, projected onto the radar's line of sight (Nevada Geodetic Laboratory).
guide.g_lim1: Motion is measured against a reference area, which may itself have moved a few centimetres.
guide.g_lim2: Water vapour delays the signal and can add a few centimetres to a date; the ionosphere is corrected, the weather only in part.
guide.g_lim3: Where the surface changes too much between passes (forest, water, the broken ground of the fault), the phase is lost and nothing is measured.
guide.i_q: How fast does the ice flow, and is it speeding up?
guide.i_aria: The same crevasses in two images weeks apart: their shift divided by the time between them is the speed of the ice.
guide.i_phys: Crevasses and dust patterns ride on the ice. Matching the same pattern in two images taken weeks apart gives how far the ice moved; divided by the time between them, its speed.
guide.i_rule1: Speed = shift ÷ time, from NASA's ITS_LIVE: optical and radar image pairs from 1985 to 2024.
guide.i_rule2: A season's speed is the median of its many pairs, so one noisy pair cannot set it.
guide.i_c_pub_d: Speeds and trends checked against those published in Nature and Nature Geoscience, for the glaciers that have them.
guide.i_c_nisar_d: Tested beside ITS_LIVE: at 12 days it does not yet resolve slow, melting glaciers, and the app says where.
guide.i_lim1: Each image pair carries its own error of tens of metres a year; on slow glaciers the speed can sit inside it.
guide.i_lim2: Speeds run from 1985 to 2024; this season's NISAR passes are counted, not yet turned into speeds.
